2.why: Modifier item: only B supplies a human agent ('conservators found') as the subject; A, C and D are all agentless and would dangle.

3.why: Split is preposition-vs-none crossed with punctuation; A keeps 'in Spain' and closes the modifying phrase with the comma the sentence needs.

4.why: Agreement pair 'have dropped'/'has dropped' is the real contrast and the odd tenses (will have, was dropping) are filler; singular 'has dropped' is the usual key.

5.why: Only the infinitive 'to present' can serve a purpose/complement slot; the nominal and finite forms are the standard non-parallel decoys.

6.why: Stem shows an appositive closed by a comma, so the blank needs singular 'work,' to match 'a sprawling epic' and pair the commas.

7.why: Pure punctuation ladder on one word; the comma is the least-marked option and the semicolon/colon require structures the other options do not hint at.

9.why: Only C makes 'the mural' the subject, which is what an introductory modifier about the mural requires; the others swap in collectors, the city, or critics.

10.why: B is the only correct colon-plus-noun-phrase; A puts a clause after the colon, C uses 'such as:', and D mixes a dash with a semicolon.

12.why: Two independent clauses around 'clarity' — the semicolon is the only joiner that works; D is a splice, B lacks the comma, A is a run-on.

14.why: Case ladder she/hers/herself/her; the nominative 'she' is the subject-slot answer and the reflexive/possessive are decoys.

15.why: Three singular verbs against one plural — 'were' is the odd one out, the shape used when an intervening phrase hides a plural subject.

16.why: Same one-plural-among-three-singular shape as 15, so 'were' is the agreement answer.

17.why: Options pair by number (are/were vs has/have); 'have' is the plural auxiliary that fits a present-perfect frame.

19.why: Past-perfect 'had lain' is required for an action completed before another past event; 'lay'/'was lying' are simple past decoys and 'has lain' is present perfect.

20.why: Infinitive 'to listen' is the only form that completes a verb complement; participles and the finite clause are the usual non-parallel distractors.
